catalog_quote: (p. 424, transcribed from page image; acute = stress as printed) 23.7. Stress. Basically, stress is assigned to the penultimate mora.[fn. 378] In the most usual case, the next to the last syllable is stressed. Thus: /ayway/ [áyway] 'go (IMP)' /aywaykan/ [aywáykaŋ] 'they are going' /aywaykanmi/ [aywaykáŋnmi] 'they are going (DIR)' /aywashaykikama/ [aywashaykikáma] 'until you go'. Since long vowels count as two mora, word-final long vowels are stressed. This may come about by (i) the final morpheme ending in an underlying long vowel or (ii) length resulting from compensatory lengthening upon the loss of a /q/: /raqa:/ [ragá:] 'abandoned house in ruins' /ama:/ [ama] 'a prehistoric people' /mana-raq/ [manárax] ~ [manará:] 'not yet' /aywa-shaq/ [aywáshax] ~ [aywashá:] 'I will go.' /chay-lla-raq/ [chayllárax] ~ [chayllará:] 'just a moment ago'. audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-sensitive, right edge, default penult, final stress only when the final vowel is long, CVV heavy / CVC light) matches Weber's explicit rule 'stress is assigned to the penultimate mora.. long vowels count as two mora, word-final long vowels are stressed', verified on the page image of the held dissertation at the cited locator (23.7, p. 424 = PDF 457, fn. 378), with the CVC-light inference supported by his own example [aywáykaŋ]/[aywaykáŋmi] and corroborated by 23.8.5 (apocope shifts stress) and 23.9.1.3 (loans take native penult stress, [bálkoŋ]). The source is the language's reference grammar by its principal describer; the only 'better' items are later editions of the same work (1989 English, 1996 Spanish), which are unlikely to change the rule. No independent phonology/instrumental study of Huallaga stress was found in Glottolog's list; web search was unavailable
